newsitem.title: CHINA: Another China interest rate cut unlikely - paper.
newsitem.headline: Another China interest rate cut unlikely - paper.

text.p: Another cut in China's interest rates, in the wake of two reductions in 1996, is unlikely this year because the shadow of inflation still lingers, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.

However, the central bank, the People's Bank of China, might make some "minor structural adjustments" to the rates on loans, it said quoting researcher Zhang Houqi of the brokerage China Securities Co Ltd.

Rumours have been rife that the central bank plans to cut interest rates in the first quarter after a soft landing in 1996 with the economy growing by 9.7 percent compared with 10.2 percent in 1995 and retail price inflation down to 6.5 percent from 14.48 percent the year before.
For the first time in 18 years, China achieved a decline in the money supply in the third quarter while maintaining strong economic momentum, the newspaper said.

The central bank may cut interest rates to help debt-laden state firms and to support economic growth, which fell 2.0 percentage points in the third quarter of last year to 9.6 percent, the newspaper quoted some analysts as saying.
However, Zhang said an interest rate cut was unlikely with the rate still close to inflation.

The 7.47 percent interest on one-year deposits was now only 1.27 percent higher than inflation but if consumer price inflation -- estimated around 8.0 percent -- was taken into account then the actual interest rate approached zero, Zhang said.
In addition, the effects of an easing of a three-year-old credit squeeze last year would only become visible this year, he said.
"The pressure of an inflationary rebound remains," he said.
He said he expected the central bank to make some slight adjustments in the lending rate, to be more flexible on loans for key projects and to pump more capital into strong-performing companies.

He said the central bank was more likely to use indirect means to control the money supply in 1997, influencing interest rates through open market operations, changes in the re-discount rate and the level of banks' reserve ratios.
